title: Vegan vs. meat: Twin brothers' six-month experiment reveals which diet packs more vitamins - The Economic Times
summary: A six-month experiment reported by The Economic Times followed twin brothers who adopted divergent diets—one vegan, one meat-inclusive—to compare vitamin status. Regular blood tests tracked nutrients such as B12, iron, vitamin D and others. The report highlighted clear differences in specific vitamins, stressed the value of careful planning or supplementation on restrictive diets, and noted that overall nutritional balance depends on food choices rather than diet labels alone.
content:
The Economic Times reported on a six-month dietary experiment involving twin brothers who intentionally followed different eating patterns to compare their vitamin profiles. One brother adopted a fully plant-based vegan diet while the other continued with a meat-inclusive omnivorous diet. Both underwent baseline blood tests and periodic monitoring to track changes in key vitamins and mineral markers.

According to the report, the study focused on commonly discussed nutrients that often differ by diet: vitamin B12, iron indices, vitamin D, folate, and certain antioxidants and phytonutrients. Monthly check-ups and dietary logs were used to verify compliance and capture any supplements or fortified foods consumed during the trial period.

Findings highlighted contrasts that nutritionists often expect: markers tied to animal-derived foods tended to be higher in the brother eating meat, whereas the vegan brother showed higher levels of some plant-derived compounds such as vitamin C and various antioxidant measures. Vitamin B12 and some iron markers were lower in the vegan participant unless fortified foods or supplements were used.

The report emphasized context and interpretation rather than declaring a single diet universally superior. It noted that differences in specific vitamin levels do not automatically translate to better or worse health outcomes without considering overall diet quality, caloric balance, lifestyle factors and medical history. Both participants reportedly adjusted intake during the trial when advised, and any supplementation was recorded as part of the study notes.

Experts quoted in the coverage cautioned against simplistic conclusions. They reiterated common public-health guidance: individuals following restrictive or highly selective diets should plan carefully to meet nutrient needs, using fortified foods or supplements when necessary, and consult healthcare providers for blood testing and personalized advice.

The story underlined practical takeaways for readers considering diet changes. For those going vegan, paying attention to B12, iron, vitamin D and omega-3 sources was advised. For omnivores, the piece recommended increasing plant variety to boost fiber, antioxidants and certain micronutrients found in fruits and vegetables.

While the experiment involved only two individuals and cannot substitute for controlled clinical trials or population studies, it offered a relatable illustration of how diet choices can influence measurable nutrient status over months. The Economic Times framed the report as a starting point for conversations about dietary planning rather than a definitive verdict on which diet "packs more vitamins."

Because detailed methodological data and raw results were not published alongside the article, readers were encouraged to interpret the findings cautiously and seek further information from peer-reviewed research before making major dietary changes.
